name: review-policy-eval-v1
description: Twenty support-desk classification items for the gateway's review/fallback policy on `POST /v1/classify` (openagents#9485). Each item is one typed question — noul, choice, or score — over one input, sent as one classify call with one unit under the mode its kind maps to: noul -> binary, choice -> single-label, score -> score. Items name a shared `sets` entry so the label set or rubric wording is identical wherever it appears. Partitions mark what the uncertainty gate should do: `answerable` items a calibrated door should answer confidently, `ambiguous` items where the honest outcome is the `uncertain` flag and a triggered review, and `near-threshold` items authored to land either side of a review cut. Labels are self-applied: every `expected` and `flag` is the suite author's own judgment, stated per item in `label_rule`; no second annotator or adjudication exists. The suite measures the policy, not the model — an item's `flag` says what the gate ought to report, and `expected` is the author's best answer even where flagging is the correct behavior.

route.description: Charges, invoices, refunds, plan pricing, and payment methods.
Product behavior that is broken, slow, or unexpected.
Sign-in, password, profile, and user-management requests.
Anything that fits none of the other teams.

severity: Cosmetic or internal only — no user-facing impact.
Minor — an inconvenience or a small subset of users affected; a workaround exists.
Major — a core workflow is impaired for many users.
Critical — the service is down, data is lost, or security is breached.
sentiment: Dissatisfied — the author is unhappy or frustrated.
Neutral — no clear sentiment either way.
Satisfied — the author is happy or complimentary.

refund-request.description: The customer asks for money back — a refund, a credit, or a reversal of a charge.

cancellation-request.description: The customer is asking to cancel their account or subscription now — not asking how cancellation works.

urgent-escalation.description: The customer demands immediate or same-day resolution, or threatens to leave.

bug-report.description: The customer reports product behavior that is broken or wrong, not a question about how a feature works.

complaint.description: The message expresses dissatisfaction with the product or the service.

items.state: I was charged twice on the March invoice and I want the duplicate charge refunded.
items.instructions: Decide what the customer is asking for.
items.label_rule: The message explicitly asks for a refund of a duplicate charge.

items.state: Where can I download a PDF copy of last month's invoice?
items.instructions: Decide what the customer is asking for.
items.label_rule: A document request with no ask for money back.

items.state: I've been going back and forth on whether to keep the subscription — what would cancelling actually involve?
items.instructions: Decide what the customer is asking for.
items.label_rule: The customer asks about the process rather than requesting it, but the wavering intent makes this a judgment a gate should flag rather than a confident no.

items.state: This has been glitchy for weeks and honestly I'm losing patience with it.
items.instructions: Decide how the customer is asking to be treated.
items.label_rule: Clear frustration but no demand, deadline, or threat; whether that counts as urgent is a genuine borderline the gate should flag.

items.state: Every so often the export button just spins — maybe one time in five, and a refresh fixes it.
items.instructions: Decide what the customer is reporting.
items.label_rule: Intermittent but clearly broken behavior; the low severity and self-fixing workaround may pull the probability near the cut.

items.state: The new dashboard is fantastic — the whole team noticed the speedup this morning.
items.instructions: Decide what the message expresses.
items.label_rule: Unambiguous praise; nothing about it is a complaint.

items.state: The charge looked wrong to me, though maybe I misread the plan terms — can someone check?
items.instructions: Decide what the customer is asking for.
items.label_rule: A verification ask, not a money-back ask — but it sits close enough to refund intent that a gate may flag it.

items.state: My invoice shows a charge from a plan I cancelled back in February.
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: An unexplained charge on an invoice is a billing matter outright.

items.state: The app crashes every single time I open the export dialog.
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: A reproducible crash is broken product behavior.

items.state: I can't sign in, and also the last invoice looks wrong — oh, and how do I add a teammate?
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: Three competing intents in one message; the author reads the sign-in lead as account work, but a correct policy flags this rather than picking confidently.

items.state: Hi — quick question about my account.
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: No actual request is stated — the mention of an account does not make it a sign-in or profile task — but the vagueness should spread the distribution and flag.

items.state: Why did my plan price change right after the trial ended?
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: A pricing question is billing work, though the account-settings framing could split the distribution near the cut.

items.state: Reports with a few thousand rows take a while to load.
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: Slow product behavior is technical work, but the mild wording could read as a general observation and sit near the cut.

items.state: How do I reset my password?
items.instructions: Route the support message to the team that should own it.
items.label_rule: A password reset is the account label's own example.

items.state: Production is down — every user sees a 500 error at sign-in and no work is getting done.
items.instructions: Rate how severe the reported issue is for the affected users.
items.label_rule: A full outage for every user is the rubric's top level by definition.

items.state: Small thing: the settings page header reads 'Prefernces'.
items.instructions: Rate how severe the reported issue is for the affected users.
items.label_rule: A typo with no functional impact is the rubric's bottom level.

items.state: Something looks off in the quarterly numbers, but I can't pin down what.
items.instructions: Rate how severe the reported issue is for the affected users.
items.label_rule: An unverifiable symptom could be cosmetic or could be data corruption; the author labels the minor level as the least-bad read while the item exists to be flagged.

items.state: The nightly sync drops a handful of files, but the morning retry always picks them up.
items.instructions: Rate how severe the reported issue is for the affected users.
items.label_rule: Real failures with a working retry sit between minor and major; the author reads minor but either side of the cut is defensible.

items.state: Absolutely loving the new release — the app has never felt this fast.
items.instructions: Rate the author's sentiment toward the product.
items.label_rule: Unqualified praise is the rubric's top level.

state.message: It's fine, I guess. The old version had its quirks too.

items.instructions: Rate the author's sentiment toward the product.
items.label_rule: Faint praise; the author reads neutral but satisfied is defensible — the record form exercises a non-text input.
